entry: Major North Vietnamese and [[Viet Cong]] offensive in the [[Vietnam War]], launched on January 30–31, 1968, against South Vietnamese, U.S., and allied forces. Its 77,000 troops struck more than 100 towns and cities, including Saigon. The offensive was a military defeat for North Vietnam, and no popular uprising followed. American public support for the war declined, and the [[Lyndon B. Johnson|Johnson]] administration sought negotiations. Shortly before the 1968 presidential election, [[Richard Nixon]] discouraged the South Vietnamese president from cooperating in the talks.

Bacterial infection, also called lockjaw, caused by *Clostridium tetani* and characterized by muscle spasms. The spasms usually begin in the jaw and then spread through the body, lasting a few minutes each and recurring for three to four weeks; some are severe enough to fracture bones. Symptoms typically begin 3 to 21 days after infection, and recovery may take months. About 10% of cases prove fatal. The bacteria usually enter through a break in the skin and produce toxins that interfere with normal muscle contractions. The disease does not spread between people and can be prevented by [[Vaccination|vaccination]]. Globally there were about 59,000 deaths in 2015, down from 356,000 in 1990.

Prehistoric [[Ocean|ocean]] that existed through much of the [[Mesozoic]] Era and the early-to-mid [[Cenozoic]] Era, lying between the continents of [[Gondwana]] and Laurasia. It was the predecessor of the modern [[Indian Ocean]] and the [[Mediterranean Sea]], and of the Eurasian inland basins now represented by the Black and Caspian seas. Collisions of the Indian, African, Australian, and Arabian plates with Eurasia in the early-mid Cenozoic raised the Alps, Himalayas, Zagros, and Caucasus mountains, and fragmented the ocean.

Organolead compound, abbreviated TEL, widely used as an antiknock additive in [[Gasoline|gasoline]] for much of the 20th century. American chemical engineer Thomas Midgley Jr. of [[General Motors]] discovered its effectiveness as a knock inhibitor on December 9, 1921. Leaded gasoline raised [[Octane rating|octane ratings]], allowing higher engine compression and better fuel economy. By the mid-20th century scientists agreed that TEL contributed to lead poisoning and was highly neurotoxic, especially in children. Most countries had banned it from gasoline by the early 2000s, and in July 2021 leaded gasoline for cars was completely phased out worldwide. It remains in some aviation fuels.

Molecular shape in which a central [[Atom|atom]] has four substituents at the corners of a [[Tetrahedron|tetrahedron]]. For a symmetric case such as [[Methane]] (CH₄), the bond angle is arccos(−1/3) = 109.4712206...° ≈ 109.5°. Methane and other perfectly symmetrical tetrahedral molecules belong to point group Td, but most tetrahedral molecules have lower symmetry, and some are chiral. Virtually all saturated organic compounds are tetrahedral, as are most compounds of silicon, germanium, and tin.

[[Polyhedron]] with four triangular faces, six straight edges, and four vertices, also called a triangular pyramid. It is the simplest ordinary convex polyhedron and the three-dimensional case of a Euclidean simplex. Any of its faces can be considered the base. A regular tetrahedron has four equilateral triangular faces and is the simplest deltahedron. Every tetrahedron has a circumsphere through its four vertices and an insphere tangent to its faces. Like all convex polyhedra, it can be folded from a single sheet of paper.

Family of marine and freshwater fish, known as pufferfish, in the order Tetraodontiformes. The name comes from the Greek *tetra*, meaning four, and *odous*, meaning tooth, for its four beak-like teeth. Pufferfish inflate their bodies with water, a defense linked to their lack of ribs, a pelvis, and pelvic fins. The family contains 193 to 206 species in 27 or 28 genera, most diverse in the tropics. Most species live in marine or brackish water, but about 35 species in several tropical genera spend their entire lives in fresh water. The majority are toxic: the liver and sometimes the skin contain tetrodotoxin, which is highly poisonous to most animals. Even so, the flesh of some species is a delicacy in [[Japan]], [[Korea]], and [[China]], when prepared by specially trained chefs.

Any [[Vertebrate|vertebrate]] of the clade Tetrapoda, comprising four-limbed animals and their descendants. The defining trait is four limbs attached to shoulder and pelvic girdles, although the group includes animals that lost their limbs, such as [[Snake|snakes]]. Tetrapods include all extant and extinct [[Amphibian|amphibians]] and amniotes. Amniotes divide into sauropsids, including reptiles, dinosaurs, and birds, and synapsids, including [[Mammal|mammals]] and their extinct relatives. Tetrapods evolved from lobe-finned fish around 390 million years ago in the Middle [[Devonian]] period, and body fossils became common around 370–360 million years ago. Amniotes include the only animals apart from insects to evolve powered flight: pterosaurs, birds, and bats.

Puzzle video game of falling pieces made of four connected blocks, called tetrominoes. Completed horizontal lines disappear, and the aim is to score as many points as possible before the stack reaches the top. Soviet software engineer Alexey Pajitnov created it in the mid-1980s while working at a computing center in [[Moscow]]. Robert Stein secured commercial rights, and Mirrorsoft and Spectrum HoloByte released the game in 1988. Henk Rogers negotiated a license with [[Nintendo]] for the [[Game Boy]] and [[Nintendo Entertainment System]], both released in 1989. The Game Boy version, which helped popularize the game, is the best-selling version, with over 35 million sales. Tetris is the best-selling video game of all time, having sold 520 million copies as of 2022.

Family of [[Insect|insects]], commonly called katydids or bush crickets. Part of the suborder Ensifera, it includes more than 8,000 known species, almost all of them in the tropics. Tettigoniids are found on every continent except Antarctica, and most are heard at night during summer and early fall. Many species are nocturnal, produce strident mating calls, and may mimic or camouflage themselves with leaflike shapes and colors. Tettigoniids range from 5 mm (1⁄4 in) to 130 mm (5 in) in length, and their filamentous antennae may exceed body length, which distinguishes them from [[Grasshopper|grasshoppers]]. Some nymphs mimic ants, spiders, or flowers until they are large enough to escape predation.

Catholic religious institution founded as a military society c. 1198 in Acre, in the [[Kingdom of Jerusalem]]. Formed to aid Christian pilgrims and establish [[Hospital|hospitals]] in the Holy Land, it also supported Catholic rule in the Holy Land and the [[Northern Crusades]]. In 1211 the order was invited to defend the [[Kingdom of Hungary]] against the [[Cumans]], but it was expelled in 1225. It then arrived in Prussia in 1230, pushed back the Prussian tribes, and created the independent State of the Teutonic Order, to which conquered territory was continuously added. Purely religious since 1810, it still confers limited honorary knighthoods, and a [[Protestantism|Protestant]] offshoot, the Bailiwick of Utrecht, also awards them.

Defunct American [[Particle accelerator|particle accelerator]] at the Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory (Fermilab) near Batavia, Illinois, operated 1983–2011. A synchrotron, it accelerated [[Proton|protons]] and antiprotons in a 6.28 km (3.90 mi) ring to energies of up to 1 TeV, hence its name. Completed in 1983 at a cost of $120 million, it was the highest-energy collider until the [[Large Hadron Collider]] at [[CERN]] near [[Geneva]], Switzerland, was built. Its main achievement was the 1995 discovery of the top quark, the last fundamental fermion predicted by the [[Standard Model]]. In 2012, analysis of around 500 trillion collisions made the existence of the [[Higgs boson]] highly likely, at a confidence of 99.8%, later improved to over 99.9%. It ceased operations on September 30, 2011, because of budget cuts and the completion of the LHC.

Ethiopian emperor (r. 1855–68). Baptized Kassa, he reunited the provinces that had fragmented during the *Zemene Mesafint*, or Era of the Princes, and is often regarded as the beginning of modern Ethiopia. He subdued Shewa and took its young prince, Sahle Maryam, into his household; the prince later became emperor as [[Menelik II]]. Tewodros established a professional standing army, salaried governors and judges, a library, tax codes, and a centralized administrative system. He sought to tax church lands, however, and his confiscation of them gained him enemies in the church and little support elsewhere. He committed suicide at the Battle of Magdala during the British Expedition to Abyssinia.

South-central [[U.S. state|state]] of the United States, second-largest by area and population. It borders Louisiana, Arkansas, Oklahoma, and [[New Mexico]], shares the Rio Grande with [[Mexico]], and has a coastline on the [[Gulf of Mexico]]. Spain was the first European power to claim it, and it became part of Mexico after independence in 1821. Tensions with settlers led to the Texas Revolution, which included the [[Battle of the Alamo]], and to the independent Republic of Texas in 1836. Texas joined the United States in 1845 as the 28th state, helping to spark the [[Mexican–American War]]. It remained a slave state until the [[American Civil War]]. Its economy is highly diversified, with energy, agriculture, technology, manufacturing, and aerospace; the [[Dallas–Fort Worth metroplex]] and Houston are its largest metropolitan areas, and Austin is the capital.

Popular variant of [[Poker|poker]] in which each player receives two hole cards and five community cards are dealt face up in three stages. Each player seeks the best five-card hand from any combination of the seven cards. Players may check, call, raise, or fold, and the best hand still in play wins the pot, which can be split on a tie. The Texas Legislature recognizes Robstown, Texas, as the birthplace of the game, dating it to the early 20th century. It was introduced to Las Vegas in 1963.

Act of composing and sending short electronic messages, typically of alphanumeric characters, between users of [[Mobile phone|mobile phones]], computers, and other devices. The term originally referred to messages sent by [[SMS|Short Message Service]] (SMS). It now includes multimedia messages with images, video, and sound, [[Emoji|emoji]], and messages sent through instant messaging apps such as [[WhatsApp]]. Texting does not require sender and recipient to be available at the same moment, which makes it useful for busy people and for interacting with automated systems, such as ordering from [[E-commerce|e-commerce]] websites. Friedhelm Hillebrand conceptualized SMS in 1984 while working for Deutsche Telekom, and his experiments with typed sentences gave the basis for the 160-character limit. The first SMS was sent on December 3, 1992.

[[Art]] made from natural or synthetic fibers, fabric, or other textiles, also called fiber art. Techniques include felting, spinning, weaving, knitting, embroidery, lace-making, dyeing, and printing. Textiles may be wall-hung, sculptural, or functional, and they have been fundamental to human life since the beginning of [[Civilization]]. The history of textile arts is also the history of [[International trade|international trade]]: [[Tyrian purple]] dye was an important trade good in the ancient Mediterranean, and the [[Silk Road]] carried Chinese silk to India, Africa, and Europe. The [[Industrial Revolution]] was shaped largely by innovations such as the cotton gin, spinning jenny, and power loom. Today the term fiber art describes textile-based decorative objects not intended for practical use.

Industry that converts [[Fiber|fibers]] into [[Yarn|yarn]], yarn into fabric, and fabric into goods such as [[Clothing|clothing]], household items, upholstery, and industrial products. Textile manufacturing evolved from household work, which was mechanized in the 18th and 19th centuries. Cotton remains the most widely used natural fiber, making up 90% of all natural fibers used in the industry. Cotton grows best in long, hot, dry summers, and at the [[Cotton gin|cotton gin]] seeds and trash are removed from the fiber; only 33% of the crop is usable lint. Yarn is then spun, woven or knitted, dyed or printed, and finished. In 2007, the global cotton yield was 25 million tons.

French Discalced Carmelite nun and [[Saint|saint]], popularly known as the Little Flower of Jesus. She entered the cloistered Carmelite community in Lisieux, [[Normandy]], at age 15, and died of [[Tuberculosis|tuberculosis]] at 24. She is one of the most popular saints in the history of the [[Catholic Church]]. Her memoir, *The Story of a Soul*, explains her Little Way of holiness through ordinary duties performed with love. [[Pope John Paul II]] declared her a Doctor of the Church in 1997. The Basilica of Lisieux is the second most popular place of pilgrimage in France, after Lourdes.

Tai language of the Kra–Dai family and sole official language of [[Thailand]]. Also called Central Thai, it is spoken by over 70 million people as of 2024 and is the most spoken of more than 60 languages in Thailand. Over half its vocabulary derives from or is borrowed from [[Pali]], [[Sanskrit]], Mon, and Old Khmer. Thai is tonal and analytic, with a complex [[Orthography|orthography]] and system of relational markers. Standard Thai, based on the dialect of the central Thai people, is the principal language of education and government and is written in the Thai script. [[Ayutthaya Kingdom|Ayutthaya]], the capital from 1351 to 1767, was bilingual in Thai and Khmer, a balance probably strengthened by Khmer captives relocated from Angkor Thom. Most minority groups are now bilingual, speaking Thai alongside their native languages.

Pre-Socratic Greek philosopher from Miletus in Ionia, one of the Seven Sages of [[Ancient Greece]]. Many regard him as the first philosopher in the Greek tradition, explaining nature through natural philosophy rather than mythology. He held that all of nature rests on a single substance, water, and that the Earth floated on water. A theorem in geometry bears his name. He was said to have calculated the heights of pyramids and the distances of ships from shore. Herodotus reports that he predicted a [[Solar eclipse|solar eclipse]] in 585 BC. He was also an engineer who enabled the [[Lydia|Lydian]] army to cross the Halys River.

Silvery-white post-transition metal, a [[Chemical element|chemical element]] with symbol Tl and atomic number 81. Thallium is not found free in nature. When isolated, it resembles tin but tarnishes in air. William Crookes and Claude-Auguste Lamy discovered it independently in 1861 by flame spectroscopy, in which thallium produces a notable green spectral line; the name comes from the Greek *thallos*, meaning green shoot. It forms +3 and +1 oxidation states, and the +1 state recalls the chemistry of [[Alkali metal|alkali metals]]. About 65% of production goes to electronics, with the rest used in pharmaceuticals and glassmaking, and it is also used in [[Infrared|infrared]] detectors. Soluble thallium salts are highly toxic and were historically used in rat poisons and insecticides, so thallium gained notoriety as the poisoner's poison.

National holiday of thanks for the harvest and the preceding year, celebrated on various dates in October and November in the [[United States]], [[Canada]], [[Saint Lucia]], and [[Liberia]]. Its roots lie in English traditions dating from the Protestant [[Reformation]], when Puritans sought to replace Church holidays with special Days of Thanksgiving and Fasting. In the United States, [[Abraham Lincoln]] proclaimed a national day of thanksgiving on October 3, 1863, and Congress fixed the holiday on the fourth Thursday of November in 1941.

Unfinished 1785 erotic novel by the [[Marquis de Sade]], set near the end of the reign of [[Louis XIV]]. Four wealthy libertines seal themselves in a castle in the [[Black Forest]] with 20 designated victims, and escalating violence leads to torture and murder. Sade believed the manuscript lost when the [[Storming of the Bastille]] took place in 1789. It survives only in draft form and was first published in a restricted edition in 1904. The novel was banned as pornographic in France and English-speaking countries, and critical opinion remains divided.

American action-adventure television series that aired on [[NBC]] from January 23, 1983, to March 8, 1987. Created by Stephen J. Cannell and Frank Lupo, *The A-Team* follows former U.S. Army Special Forces soldiers, falsely convicted of a crime, who escape military prison and become soldiers of fortune dedicated to helping those in need. The show is known for cartoonish violence, formulaic episodes, and improvised weaponry. It boosted the career of [[Mr. T]], who played B. A. Baracus. A feature film based on the series was released by 20th Century Fox in 2010.
